summary: Asks IANA to create a registry for PIM message types, lists initial contents from existing RFCs and sets a registration procedure. It also reserves one type for future extension. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 8736.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6166 creates a registry for PIM message types and lists the initial assignments. It also sets a review process for new values and reserves one value for a possible extension.

questions: what is the pim message type registry
which pim message type is reserved
subtitle: Creates an IANA registry for Protocol Independent Multicast message types.

tldr.problem: PIM version 2 message types were specified in several documents without a separate registry to record them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC establishes a four-bit message type registry, records the initial values, sets IETF Review for new types, and reserves type 15 for a future extension.

today: RFC 6166 was obsoleted by RFC 8736, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why PIM Needed a Registry
sections.content: PIM version 1 used IGMP and had message types listed in an IGMP registry. PIM version 2 is not based on IGMP, while several RFCs define PIM version 2 message types. RFC 6166 creates a separate registry to list those types and provide a process for registering new ones.
sections.plainLanguage: PIM version 2 uses its own message types, defined across several RFCs. This RFC gives them a dedicated list.

sections.title: The Registry and Initial Values
sections.content: The PIM message type field is four bits, with possible values from 0 to 15. The initial registry assigns types 0 through 10 to named messages, leaves 11 through 14 unassigned, and reserves 15 for a future extension of the type space. New message types are assigned through IETF Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The four-bit field has values from 0 to 15. The registry records assigned types, leaves some unassigned, and reserves one for future extension.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that a well-known place to find valid PIM message types and how they are used may provide a security benefit. Apart from that, the document creates an IANA registry and has no security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared list can help readers identify valid message types. The RFC says it adds no other security considerations.
